entry.dc:title: Unusually physical and chemical characteristics of oil sands from Qaidam basin, NW China
entry.dc:creator: Gao Z.N.
entry.prism:publicationName: Geochemical Journal
entry.dc:description: Gas chromatography (GC), gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC/MS), supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC), elemental analysis, infrared absorption spectroscopy (IR), thermal analysis (TG/DTA), Rock-Eval pyrolysis, as well as viscosity and density analysis revealed that oil sands from Qaidam basin, Qinghai Province of China, are highly concentrated in light components (≤C<inf>23</inf>), with saturated hydrocarbons (including most n-alkanes) comprising between 49.6 to 71.4% of total organics (wt.%). Their physicochemical characteristics are very similar to those of heavy oils, rather than other oil sand bitumens. The above analyses suggest that Qinghai oil sands originate from a terrigenous source, similar to oils from the surrounding area. Additionally, the existence of n-alkanes shows that the oil sands are weakly biodegraded, and that the formation of these unusual oil sands is related to the particular geographic/climatic conditions of Qaidam basin. No other known oil sands with chemical composition and distribution similar to that in Qinghai have been documented. Exploitation should be initiated with drilling wells followed by open pit mining. entry.dc:title: Contract versus owner mining - An update on Australasian open pit mining practice
entry.dc:creator: Dunlop J.S.F.
entry.prism:publicationName: Institution of Mining and Metallurgy Transactions Section A Mining Technology
entry.dc:description: With the advent of the resources' boom in the late 1960s, most of the larger scale resources projects in Australasia were commissioned on an 'owner-mining' basis, where the mine owners owned and operated the primary mining equipment. Then, in the 1980s with the arrival of the gold mining boom in Western Australia and elsewhere, a change occurred - most of the mining activities were carried out on a contract mining basis. Over recent years, however, there has been a marked trend amongst larger Australasian open pit mining operations back towards owner-controlled and operated mining operations. The reasons for this are many and are addressed in the paper, but centre on the concept of the owner being prepared to assume more of the mining risk in exchange for the advantage of not having to pay a contractor's profit margin. Where mining contracts are entered into, the older 'schedule of rates' format is being replaced with less adversarial and more entrepreneurial contract alternatives involving operating cost and risk sharing in a spirit of'fair dealing'. Leasing and maintenance issues have also been influenced in recent years by the advent of more flexible contract arrangements with equipment suppliers. Group purchasing has also had some influence for project operators. For many mine owners, the optimal risk management profile involves a practical off-setting of the assumption of mining risk on the one hand, against the removal of litigation risk and potentially reduced operating costs on the other. Potential pitfalls may arise where equipment size and type requirements vary with time or where manpower management, mining flexibility, job skills or safety exposure factors are relevant. These issues are commented on in the context of some well-known examples, and an update is provided on contract mining versus owner operation in large scale Australasian open pit mining generally. © 2005 IoM Communications Ltd.

entry.dc:title: Open pit optimisation including mineral dressing criteria using 0-1 non-linear goal programming
entry.dc:creator: Esfandiari B.
entry.prism:publicationName: Institution of Mining and Metallurgy Transactions Section A Mining Technology
entry.dc:description: Proper production scheduling and open pit mining designs are the most important factor for improving productivity. Some mining mathematical models can obtain the optimised production scheduling and the final pit limits as single objective function. In this work, an attempt is made by using the multiple criteria decision-making model and zero-one non-linear goal programming to derive production scheduling as effective ways to achieve higher profits in a prc-assumcd time span and under specific economic and technical considerations. Applying simulation methods for construction of a virtual mine and comparing the obtained results with those of a real open pit (the Jalal-Abad Ironstone mine which was designed using of widely known and acceptable mining design software), the proposed model's accuracy is assessed. © 2005 IoM Communications Ltd.

entry.dc:title: Jamaican deforestation and bauxite mining - The role of negotiations for sustainable resource use
entry.dc:creator: Berglund C.
entry.prism:publicationName: Minerals and Energy Raw Materials Report
entry.dc:description: Bauxite mining is considered to be one of the most significant reasons behind deforestation in Jamaica. During the last decades, large areas of forest have been cleared on the island due' to open pit mining for bauxite. Because private landowners own the bauxite land, the operating mining companies are in many cases forced to bargain with the private landowners to obtain access to the desired land. Several economic theories present solutions to the problem of sustainable resource use. The purpose of this paper is to examine if the Coase theorem can be applied to analyze if the deforestation caused by bauxite mining in Jamaica can be amended towards optimal resource management. The paper concludes that there exist no practical obstacles for bargaining to take place. However, since the market for bauxite mining is not characterized by perfect competition, an efficient allocation of the Jamaican forests according to the Coase theorem is not achieved. Yet we find that the antiquated Coase theorem can help us gain knowledge into some fundamental aspects of the prevailing market conditions surrounding Jamaican bauxite mining. © 2004 Taylor and Francis.

entry.dc:title: The jewel in the crown
entry.prism:publicationName: Mining Magazine
entry.dc:description: Carajas (Brazil) is one of the world's most important mineral provinces. The iron ore production complex in Carajas includes the simultaneous operation of four open pit mines; the N4E, N4WN, N5E and N5W mines. Among these mines, N4E is not only the largest but also the oldest. Open pit mining operation with the use of trucks and shovels at N4E started in 1984. Ore is treated through crushing and screening. Generally, N4E contributes a significant amount to the total 25 Mt/y of run-of-mine production in the Carajas complex.

entry.dc:title: Mining and regional development in Peru
entry.dc:creator: Golte J.
entry.prism:publicationName: Geographische Rundschau
entry.dc:description: Mining has a 4000 years old history in the Central Andes. In the time of the Viceroyalty of Peru the mining of silver and gold has been the centre of spatial organization of different types of production (agriculture and manufacture) and forced labour services of the indigenous population. The outdated colonial mining techniques led to a virtual collapse of the mining sector with the independence of Peru. After 1850 the mining sector recovered with labour intensive exploitation of silver, iron, copper and gold deposits. The salaries for the unskilled labour force recruited in surrounding Indian communities led to a slow development of the hinterland of the mining centres. The revenue for the Peruvian state on the other hand resulted in an increasing service economy in Lima depending on the redistribution of tax income through the state to a privileged sector of the population. Modern open pit mining in Peru is globally competitive and contributes to more than 50 % of Peruvian exports. Due to the consumption of the revenue by a privileged social sector and the increasing industrialization of the mining process (with a small and academically educated labour force) with little impact on the regional population the lucrative ore mines are nowadays surrounded by impoverished peasants. So the mining industry, technically efficient, is confronted ever more by social unrest.

entry.dc:title: Efficiency of a Bucket Wheel Excavator lignite mining system
entry.dc:creator: Kolovos C.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: Bucket Wheel Excavator (BWE) based systems are used worldwide in open pit mining of soft to medium hard rock materials such as lignite, phosphate, etc. This paper presents a 15-year analysis of actual performance data of a Greek, medium-sized, lignite open pit mine. In this mine, BWEs are used for the continuous, selective mining of lignite. Conveyor belts are used for transporting the excavated material to stackers at the lignite stockyards or to the waste dumping sites. The basic excavation equipment had already been used in another mine. As a result, the BWEs examined are rather old machines and their combined service life has exceeded 40 years. Remarkably, no decrease in the overall performance was observed and further utilization of these BWEs is scheduled.

entry.dc:title: Tire Awareness Program
entry.dc:creator: Tattersall A.
entry.prism:publicationName: Engineering and Mining Journal
entry.dc:description: Tire awareness program, a program started by the Coeur Rochester company with the assistance of the Elite Tire Management System (ETMS) to improve the performance of tires is discussed. After using this program the improvement acheived in tire life over the haulage and loading fleets have ranged from 11% to 45% without any effect on quality. The efforts to improve tire performance are directed at all members of the tire team, including management and supervision. The program focuses on the tire use and abuse and is equally applicable to the full range of performances in open pit mining or in any other industrial operation.

entry.dc:title: Sizing equipment for open pit mining - A review of critical parameters
entry.dc:creator: Bozorgebrahimi E.
entry.prism:publicationName: Institution of Mining and Metallurgy Transactions Section A Mining Technology
entry.dc:description: Over the past century, open pit mines have steadily increased their production rate. Larger equipment and new technologies make it possible to mine larger batches of materials in a shorter time. Low commodity prices have forced companies to decrease their unit cost, by using new technologies and improving productivity. In the late 20th century, with companies facing low commodity prices and competing with strong rivals globally, larger equipment with lower unit costs ensured survival. As a result, mine geometry and mining equipment have dramatically increased in size. To date, in terms of productivity, the mining industry continues to adhere to the 'bigger is better' mentality. There are indications that this strategy may not always be advantageous. This paper will discuss on-going research into understanding the effects of equipment size on surface mining. The research includes investigation of mine and mill construction and operating costs, mine productivity, mine design, and economic optimisation. It identifies the significant variables that need to be considered and suggests an approach to quantify their impact on the mine. The paper also proposes a new view to mine planning and equipment selection with respect to the sensitivity to equipment size factors. © 2003 IoM Communications Ltd.

entry.dc:title: Reliability modelling of surface mining equipment: Data gathering and analysis methodologies
entry.dc:creator: Hall R.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: As the size and complexity of open pit mining equipment continue to increase, the implications of equipment failure become ever more critical. An unplanned failure can result in significantly higher repair costs than a planned maintenance or repair. Of even more importance is the loss of production associated with larger equipment failures. One method to mitigate the impact of failures is to improve the reliability of the equipment. A first step in reliability improvement is collection and analysis of the appropriate data. This paper will summarize relevant techniques for reliability analysis and identify data requirements and information sources.

entry.dc:title: Thermal rock fragmentation - Applications in narrow-vein extraction
entry.dc:creator: Poirier S.
entry.prism:publicationName: CIM Bulletin
entry.dc:description: This paper focusses on new developments regarding thermal rock fragmentation applications. The technology consists of a strong burner powered by diesel fuel and air. The thermal reaction that is created allows for the enlargement of 125 mm to 450 mm holes by breaking the rock in a spalling effect. It has been used for over 30 years in Russian open pit mining. Following an agreement between Dynamitage T.C.G. Inc. and the owner of the technology, major improvements have been brought to this technology, allowing for the fabrication of a prototype suitable for the Canadian industry. In Russia and the Ukraine, thermal rock fragmentation is actually used to drill large diameter holes in surface mining. Upon having acquired a better knowledge of this technology, it seems that it presents a great potential for selective mining in narrow-vein operations, for either surface or underground mining. Rocmec International Inc., a subsidiary of Dynamitage T.C.G. Inc., and Natural Resources Canada are technical partners in the evaluation of the operational parameters and environmental aspects such as gas, heat, dust and fog emissions. Furthermore, Canada Economic Development is a financial partner in this project. This paper presents the technology and its history. It also reports on the changes brought to the equipment to adapt it to North American environments. A summary of the tests carried out since 1995 is provided, along with the main conclusions obtained. The anticipated applications for the use of this technology in both surface and underground environments are described such as open pit mining, bulk sampling and narrow-vein ore extraction. An estimate showing a comparison between the thermal fragmentation mining concept and the long-hole mining method is presented and, finally, the future developments planned are listed.
entry.authkeywords: Bulk sampling | Drilling | Narrow-vein extraction | Open pit mining | Rock breaking | Thermal rock fragmentation

entry.dc:title: Recultivation of gravel pits and quarries in Lower Saxony
entry.dc:creator: Fahlbusch M.
entry.prism:publicationName: Erzmetall Journal for Exploration Mining and Metallurgy
entry.dc:description: The determination of the requirements for recultivation plays a crucial role in the statutory licensing procedure for the open pit mining of non-metallic minerals. In recent years, a working aid has been developed for the application of control regulations for environmental protection in raw material mining proposals in Lower Saxony. Since the licensing authorities of the individual counties proceeded very differently, the goal was to achieve a uniform state-wide regulation with regard to the scope of recultivation measures to be carried out. The plan of the working aid was submitted in 1999 by Lower Saxony's Department of Environmental Protection and subsequently revised over several years in a referendum process which included the industry. The paper should be valid for licensing procedures according to State Environmental Protection Law and State Water Law. The working aid should be regarded as a technical standard in licensing procedures which are carried out according to other specialized legislation such as the Federal Mining Law and the Federal Law for Emission Protection. The organization of the contents of the working aid and the steps to be carried out are illustrated within the framework of this paper. Using unconsolidated and solid rock mining as an example, the requirements for recultivation which result from the application of the working aid are explained.
entry.authkeywords: Consolidated rock | Environmental protection | Non-metallic minerals | Recultivation | Unconsolidated rock

entry.dc:title: The Grande Cache Coal project
entry.dc:creator: Cain P.
entry.prism:publicationName: CIM Bulletin
entry.dc:description: Grande Cache Coal (GCC), an investor-owned Alberta company, is in the final stages of the regulatory process leading to the resumption of coal mining in the Smoky River Coal Field of Alberta. Although many opportunities for low-cost, high-yield mining remained on the property, GCC opted for a long-term production plan that ensures stability for the local economy, sustainable use of the resources in the area, environmental responsibility and a satisfactory return for its investors. GCC entered the Alberta coal approval process in late 2000 with a public disclosure document. In October 2001, GCC formally submitted an application for mining approval and an environmental impact assessment (EIA) to the government and the public. The application covered the proposed Grande Cache Coal project, which includes the No. 7 underground mine, No. 8 surface mine and coal processing operations. The EIA provided a comprehensive investigation of environmental sensitivities in the project area, matched with environmental protection programs. The project is based on commencement of operations in late 2002. GCC's plans are founded on a commitment to sustainable development and has framed this commitment in the context of a long-range mine development plan that will sustain the community of Grande Cache over the next 25 years. The Grande Cache coalfields offer extensive coal reserves and opportunities, for both surface and underground mining. Combining highly productive U.S.-style room-and-pillar underground mining methods and conventional truck-and-shovel open pit mining, GCC's approach to sustainable development encompasses community involvement and reclamation of mine sites to productive land uses after mining.

entry.dc:title: Characterization of suspended particulate matter in mining areas in São Paulo, Brazil
entry.dc:creator: Almeida I.T.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: Atmospheric pollution aspects in mining are analyzed. Two types of environment have been selected for study: an open pit mining site and a quarry. In order to obtain a preliminary evaluation of the air quality in these environments, a sampling program was developed for each area. Three basic points were studied: 1. Concentration of total suspended particulate; 2. Chemical and 3. Physical characterization of the particulate matter. The concentrations of total suspended particulate (TSP) were obtained by the use of the high volume sampler method. The analytic techniques applied to the particulate matter were X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) for chemical characterization, and Low Angle Laser Light Scattering (LALLS) for physical characterization. Physical characterization involved particle size distribution of the suspended particulate matter, whereas the chemical characterization involved determination of its composition.

entry.dc:title: Expert system for equipment selection
entry.dc:creator: Ganguli R.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: An expert system was developed for equipment selection for various unit operations in open pit mining. For each unit operation, it considers a wide variety of equipment and ranks them based on their suitability. A major difference between this system and other published expert systems in the considered domain is that it incorporates the uncertainty that is an inherent characteristic of the factors affecting equipment selection. It also allows users to specify the site-specific relative importance of each of the governing factors. This makes the system relatively flexible and allows its adaptation to different mining conditions. The programming features of the expert system include uncertainty databases and object oriented programming. The expert system is validated with a case study (Malanjkhand Copper Mine, India).

entry.dc:title: Slide cam compound grease lubricant: Development and field evaluation
entry.dc:creator: Samman N.
entry.prism:publicationName: NLGI Spokesman
entry.dc:description: Walking draglines in open pit mining have unique lubrication requirements. The lubrication requirements of the Bucyrus-Erie (BE) cam and slide walking cam mechanism used on some walking draglines are considered. The evolution of walking cam lubricants is outlined. The development of summer and winter grade grease lubricants for the BE cam and slide walking cam mechanism is described. Slide rig testing and field trials with the lubricants are reported. The lubricants met the desired lubrication performance in mine site operations.

entry.dc:title: Rock fall in surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Brawner C.O.
entry.prism:publicationName: CIM Bulletin
entry.dc:description: The classical approach to control rock fall and ravel in open pit mining has been to use catch benches. The width and volume of benches is most dependent on the bench height, size of loading equipment, blast damage to the face and mining regulations. This was compatible with open pit slopes of less than approximately 45 degrees. As our understanding of rock mechanics and blasting control has improved over recent years, much steeper rock slopes can be developed at many open pit mines. However, narrower benches result in less rock fall capacity. The transportation industry has been very successful in using catch fences to protect highways throughout North America and Europe for years. The authors recommend that cable and ring net fences have a potential major application in open pit mining to allow steeper rock slopes with significant economic benefit. This paper outlines the application, design and operation of catch fences in surface mining for specific conditions. Typical case examples are presented.
entry.authkeywords: Blasting | Catch fences | Rock mechanics | Surface mining

entry.dc:title: Ambient air quality in the bauxite mining area of Yercaud hills in Eastern Ghats
entry.dc:creator: Muthusubramanian P.
entry.prism:publicationName: Indian Journal of Environmental Protection
entry.dc:description: The Sheveroys also known as Yercaud hills, the presnt study area, are situated to the north east of Salem city in the state of Tamil Nadu of India and form a major hill range at the southern most point of the Eastern Ghats. The biosphere reserves of this region are threatened due to mining and deforestation acivities. The bauxite of Shevaroy hill is being exploited for aluminium production. Bauxite production is through open pit mining. The objective of this present study is to assess the impact of bauxite mining on the quality of air in the Yercaud hills for all seasons of the year 1997. For air sampling 4 vantage points were selected and fixed for the continuous monitoring of the air quality aid meteorological parameters, such as temperature, humidity, wind speed and wind direction, both inside and outside of mines for all the seasons in a year. The samples were collected weekly at all the 4 sites by drawing a known volume of air through a membrane of glass microfibre filter for 8 hr using a high volume sampler to estimate the concentration levels of sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide and suspended particulate matter (SPM). It is found that at all the sites and seasons, the concentration levels of these air pollutants are within the permissible limits. The reasons for the variation of concentration levels of these pollutants with respect to sites and seasons are discussed.

entry.dc:title: "Natura 2000" - Impact on the mining of deposits near the surface
entry.dc:creator: Fahlbusch M.
entry.prism:publicationName: Erzmetall Journal for Exploration Mining and Metallurgy
entry.dc:description: The European environmental protection legislation has had the effect of complicating mining of deposits near the surface in Europe. The Union's "Natura 2000" programme is a current topic of discussion. - The creation of "Natura 2000" brings with it nature conservation areas for certain ecosystems and animals as well as the conservation areas for certain birds. Additional nature conservation areas, based on the Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora and the Council Directive 79/409/EEC of 2 April 1979 on the conservation of wild birds, will further limit the surface area available for mining of raw materials. The large-area environmental protection intended by "Natura 2000" presents particular problems for the mining of raw materials, which depends on connected areas. - In some cases, mining of raw materials itself is fundamentally questioned through "Natura 2000". At the very least, "Natura 2000" means significant additional expenditure in the fields of project planning, operation and recultivation of open pit mining operations. - The effects of the "Natura 2000" should be avoided. In addition to the traditional geological, technical and economical restrictions of mining planning, new planning restrictions are added which, when left unconsidered, would force a mining project to be unauthorized.

entry.dc:title: Coalbed methane prospect of Jamalganj coalfield, Bangladesh
entry.dc:creator: Imam M.B.
entry.prism:publicationName: Arabian Journal for Science and Engineering
entry.dc:description: Five major Gondwana coalfields have been discovered in the half-graben type basins in the subsurface in the Precambrian platform area of northwest Bangladesh. The Jamalganj coalfield, with an estimated reserve of about 1053 million tons of coal, has seven coal seams in the depth range between 640 to 1158 m below the ground surface. Compared to the other coalfields of the area, with coal occurring at 150 to 500 m depth, Jamalganj coal is considered to be too deep to be exploited by conventional underground or open pit mining. Instead, developing coal bed methane from Jamalganj coalfield may be considered as a viable option for its exploitation. The positive factors of Jamalganj coal bed methane development include high net thickness of coal with at least one very thick (40 m+) and widely developed seam, coal seam burial depth within optimum range, large coal reserves, indication of significant gas content from drilling data, and poor permeability in the rocks above and surrounding the coal layers. The thickest seam III can be a primary target for CBM development especially where it combines with seam IV in the eastern part of the coalfield. However, there are a number of unknown factors like actual gas content of coal, the coal permeability, and in-seam pressure that need to be evaluated before deciding the viability of the project. An initial attempt to collect these baseline data should include drilling test well or wells in the primary target area where seam III is most thick and widely developed.

entry.dc:title: A simulative model for optimum open pit design
entry.dc:creator: Erarslan K.
entry.prism:publicationName: CIM Bulletin
entry.dc:description: Previous research in the area of open pit mine optimization has focused on profit maximization by optimizing pit limits or optimizing production schedules. However, these two approaches are interrelated and dependent on each other. Recent studies have recognized the limitation of this optimization approach. Consequently, there is a need for a more comprehensive modelling strategy. Such an optimization model should incorporate mining activities that are simulated (as they are expected to occur) as much as possible. Considerations should be given to such parameters as the cut-off ore grade, the starting location of mining, equipment selection, annual production rates, excavation sequence, and the synchronization of the mining plant operations during the planning stage of the mine. A change in any of these parameters will cause a concomitant change in other parameters. Therefore an efficient optimization system is one that attempts to simulate the mine in a comprehensive manner and thereby provides more realistic results. In this study, a new profit maximization model that determines optimum pit limit as a function of optimum production scheduling has been developed. The model allows for the progressive addition of new ore blocks as well as for process plant feeding. The model gives realistic estimates of the unit cost for each new condition of the pit as part of an overall economic analysis of the integrated mining and ore processing operation. Optimization of the entire mining operation is achieved through the minimization of idle times of the processing plant and through maintaining a uniform ore feed to the processing plant. The proposed model has been programmed in C++, and it has been used to analyze a number of typical open pit mining scenarios. The results obtained using the model have proved the validity of this new modelling approach.
entry.authkeywords: Dynamic programming | Mine simulation | Optimum pit design | Profit maximization
